m7-t1.question: Why did the photographer with 2,400 emails out-book the one with 18,000 followers?
options: Her photos were better
Email is owned land — 2,400 × 95% delivery reached more humans than 18,000 × 7% algorithmic reach
Instagram had banned the other photographer
Emails cost less to send than posts
m7-t1.explanation: Social reach is rented and throttled; the email list is owned, with stable delivery — a smaller list can out-reach a big following.

m7-t1.question: What is email marketing's strategic job in the funnel?
options: Top-of-funnel discovery and cold reach
Retention and repeat — turning one-time buyers into repeat customers and enquiries into bookings
Replacing paid advertising entirely
Search engine visibility
m7-t1.explanation: Acquisition happens elsewhere; email multiplies what acquisition brings — the second half of the funnel.

m7-t1.question: Which list practice is BOTH legally toxic and a deliverability killer?
options: Sending a weekly newsletter
Buying an email list
Removing hard bounces
Using a signup form with an unchecked box
m7-t1.explanation: Bought lists carry unprovable consent and spam traps — exposure plus a throttled domain.

m7-t1.question: Which of the five fundamental emails is typically the MOST opened you will ever send?
options: The monthly offer
The win-back email
The welcome email, sent immediately on signup
The thank-you email
m7-t1.explanation: The welcome email hits the peak-attention window and often earns 50%+ opens — deliver the promised resource, set expectations.

m7-t1.question: Which metric is the honest KPI of email performance, and why?
options: Open rate — it measures attention
Delivery rate — it proves deliverability
Click rate — opens are inflated by auto-open behaviour, clicks drive action
List size — reach is everything
m7-t1.explanation: Healthy clicks run 2–5%; Apple Mail auto-opens distort open rates, making clicks the decision-grade number.

m7-t2.question: What is the correct first step when designing an automated journey?
options: Open the tool and start dragging blocks
Draw it on paper — boxes and arrows, every branch labelled
Write all the email copy
Buy a bigger plan for branching features
m7-t2.explanation: Undrawn journeys become unfixable hairballs; the map IS the automation plan.

m7-t2.question: In a welcome series, what does email 3 (around day 5) deliver in the lesson's structure?
options: The biggest discount of the year
Social proof — testimonials, results, UGC
A survey asking why they haven't bought
The origin story of the founder
m7-t2.explanation: Day 0 delivers the promise, day 2 builds relationship (origin/difference), day 5 proves with social proof, day 10 makes the soft offer.

m7-t2.question: What ends a healthy win-back series?
options: A fourth, fifth and sixth offer with bigger discounts
A goodbye 'should we part ways?' email, then exit and suppress
Moving them to the daily newsletter
A phone call from the owner
m7-t2.explanation: Three emails, then dignity: the goodbye email either revives or cleans the list — unending win-backs train people to ignore you.

m7-t2.question: Which behavioural-trigger email crosses the creep line?
options: Still thinking it over? Here's the demo video again
Your cart is waiting — complete in one click
We saw you staring at the ₹499 package for six minutes
Seats for the batch you viewed are filling up
m7-t2.explanation: Trigger on what they did, speak to what they want, never narrate the watching — surveillance is not service.

m7-t2.question: How should a JOURNEY's health be judged?
options: By the open rate of its best single email
By completion rate, drop-off step, and goal conversions per entrant
By total emails sent
By unsubscribe count alone
m7-t2.explanation: A great email 2 with 70% drop-off at email 1 is a bad journey — measure the flow, not the parts.

m7-t3.question: In plain terms, what is a CRM?
options: An email-sending platform with templates
A shared memory with discipline: every person, status, history and next action with an owner and date
A sales forecasting AI
A customer-facing chat widget
m7-t3.explanation: Columns like Name, Source, Stage, Next step, Owner — everything else is decoration on those bones.

m7-t3.question: What design rule keeps a pipeline honest?
options: Use as many stages as the tool allows
Copy the enterprise default pipeline exactly
Written stage definitions plus lost-with-reason for every deal that dies
Let each salesperson interpret stages their own way
m7-t3.explanation: Undefined stages let everyone interpret 'qualified' their way — and the lost-reason list becomes marketing's feedback loop.

m7-t3.question: A lead has: referral source (+20), clicked the pricing page (+20), asked 'when can we start?' (+25), opened 2 nurture emails (+10). Under the lab's scoring, how is it routed?
options: C-lead — automated nurture only
B-lead — nurture plus a weekly touch
A-lead — personal call within 24 hours
Discard — the score is too high to be real
m7-t3.explanation: 75 points ≥ 60 = A-lead: speed beats polish; a decent call today outsells a perfect call Friday.

m7-t3.question: What does the research-backed follow-up discipline say?
options: Most enquiries convert on the first contact, so one polished call is enough
Most converting enquiries take a second or later contact — yet most businesses stop after one
Follow up daily forever until they buy
Wait a week between touches to seem uninterested
m7-t3.explanation: Mechanical cadence with an end: day 0 call, day 1 WhatsApp, day 3 call + case study, day 7 email, day 14 close-file — then Lost-with-reason.

m7-t3.question: When should a small business buy a full-featured CRM suite?
options: Immediately — better tooling creates better process
Only when the process has outgrown the sheet/lightweight tool; adoption beats features
When the free trial expires
Never; spreadsheets are always enough
m7-t3.explanation: Buying Stage 2 tooling for a Stage 0 process produces an expensive spreadsheet — the tool should take LESS time than the diary it replaces.

m7-t4.question: What is the DPDP Act 2023's core requirement for processing personal data in India?
options: Only companies above 500 employees need consent
Notice and consent for specified purposes, with rights to access, correct and erase
Data can be used for any purpose once collected
Consent is only needed for foreign users
m7-t4.explanation: Purpose limitation plus data-principal rights — the 'we'll also text them about anything' habit is now a liability.

m7-t4.question: Which consent type is 'gold' for marketing?
options: Explicit opt-in via an unchecked box or signup form
Implied consent from an order confirmation
Bundled consent in the terms of service
Consent purchased with a list
m7-t4.explanation: Explicit opt-in is recorded, purpose-limited, and withdrawable — the foundation of a clean, deliverable channel.

m7-t4.question: What must an unsubscribe link do to be compliant?
options: Require login to confirm identity first
Ask three survey questions, then process within 30 days
Work in one click, honoured immediately, present in every email
Redirect to a retention offer page with no exit
m7-t4.explanation: Instant, frictionless withdrawal is a legal expectation and a mailbox-rule requirement — walls before the exit are a failure mode.

m7-t4.question: Which five-sentence privacy notice structure does the lesson recommend?
options: Legalese definitions, jurisdiction clauses, arbitration terms
Who we are and what we collect; why; who else sees it; how long and how to erase; how to withdraw consent
A single line: 'We respect your privacy'
A link to the government's website
m7-t4.explanation: A notice people can read is a notice that protects — name the tools, name the contact, commit to the deletion window.

m7-t4.question: Which is one of the seven failure modes the lesson warns about?
options: Sending a weekly newsletter
Purpose creep — collecting data for orders, then using it for unrelated promotions
Using an email tool with built-in templates
Asking for a phone number on a contact form
m7-t4.explanation: Purpose creep, bundled consent, pre-ticked boxes, broken unsubscribes, no records, scraped lists, invisible grievance routes — the seven sinkholes.

questions.question: A business's email open rate is 38% but its click rate is 0.4%. What is the correct diagnosis and action?
options: Great opens mean the strategy works; keep going
Subject lines earn opens but the body fails its promise — no clear single CTA, no value in the email; restructure around one idea and one CTA
The list is too small; buy more contacts
Switch to a more expensive email tool
questions.explanation: Clicks are the honest KPI (2–5% healthy): high opens plus dead clicks means the email is a brochure with a good headline.

questions.question: A coaching centre wants mid-funnel leads to stop going cold. Which build is correct?
options: Add them to the monthly newsletter and hope
A 4–6 email nurture journey, one objection per email, with a behavioural branch: pricing-page clicks routed to a personal call within 24 hours
A win-back series with escalating discounts
Daily promotional emails until they enrol
questions.explanation: Nurture answers objections in sequence; behavioural triggers hand hot leads to humans — journey machinery plus CRM memory.

questions.question: Of 240 enquiries in a term, 96 were called back. Which system failure does this reveal?
options: A channel-mix failure — the ads targeted the wrong people
A memory failure — no CRM, no owner, no next-action-with-date; enquiries live in inboxes and die
A creative failure — the ads over-promised
A pricing failure — the fee was too high
questions.explanation: Every enquiry recorded, every conversation logged, every next step owned — the CRM externalises memory so leads cannot rot.

questions.question: A startup scraped 40,000 WhatsApp contacts and blasted a launch email. Their domain got throttled. What caused it?
options: The email was too long
Unprovable consent plus spam complaints — spam-complaint rates above 0.3% get domains throttled by mailbox providers
They sent at the wrong time of day
The subject line was in English
questions.explanation: Mailbox rules (authentication, one-click unsubscribe, complaint rates) bite faster than regulators — the list shortcut destroyed the channel.

questions.question: A term's lost-reason data shows 'fee too high' in 60% of losses. What is the correct marketing conclusion?
options: Reduce the fee by 60%
The offer design (packaging, instalments, value framing) needs work — not necessarily the price itself
Increase the ad budget to offset losses
Stop tracking lost reasons; they demotivate the team
questions.explanation: Lost-with-reason is the feedback loop: when one reason dominates, the fix lives in offer design, not louder acquisition.

questions.question: Welcome email 1 gets 55% opens; email 2 drops to 12%. What should you examine first?
options: The subject line of email 2 and whether it arrives at the promised cadence with real value
Whether to delete email 2 entirely
The unsubscribe rate of email 1
The sending domain's DMARC record
questions.explanation: Drop-off at email 2 is the classic journey failure: the relationship email must earn its place, not just occupy day 2.

questions.question: A client asks you to email everyone who bought from them three years ago, 'they won't mind.' What is the professional answer?
options: Send it — past customers are always fair game
It depends: consent likely expired for unrelated promotions; re-permission with a short 'do you still want to hear from us?' email, and suppress non-responders
Send it but hide the unsubscribe link to protect the list
Refuse; email can never be used on old customers
questions.explanation: Purpose and time limits matter; a re-permission campaign either revives the relationship or cleans the list — both wins.

questions.question: A business wants 'one CRM for everything' but has 30 leads a month and a two-person team. What do you recommend?
options: An enterprise suite for future-proofing
A Stage-0 sheet CRM with dropdowns, scoring columns and a weekly review ritual — upgrade when the process outgrows it
No system; memory and WhatsApp suffice at this size
A CRM plus an automation consultant
questions.explanation: The tool should take less time than the diary it replaces; adoption beats features, and the ritual is the system.

questions.question: A nurture journey branches: clicked pricing twice → personal call; no opens → slower cadence. What principle does the branch demonstrate?
options: Bundled consent
Behavioural triggers route human attention where it pays — the machinery watches so people can sell
Vanity-metric optimisation
Last-click attribution
questions.explanation: The journey is the machinery, the CRM is the memory — automation decides WHO gets human effort, not whether humans matter.

questions.question: Under DPDP-era practice, what must accompany a signup form's data collection?
options: Nothing; collection is free by default
Clear notice of what will be sent and how often, an unchecked consent box, and a genuinely working exit — with records of when and how consent was given
Only a privacy policy link in the footer
A phone-number field for verification
questions.explanation: Notice, opt-in, easy withdrawal, and provable records — the four props that keep both the regulator and the mailbox providers happy.
